# Bharujātaka (Ja 213)

**ID:** Ja 213
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bharujātaka* (Ja 213) is a two-verse narrative preserved within the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali Canon [Fausböll 1879]. According to the commentary's nidāna, the Buddha delivered this teaching while staying at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī, addressing King Pasenadi of Kosala regarding the perils of bribery and inciting discord between rival groups of ascetics [Tan 2002; Fausböll 1879].

The canonical text comprises two gāthās (verses 124–125) [Fausböll 1879]. The opening verse recalls the fate of King Bharu (*Bharurājā*), ruler of the Bharu kingdom (*Bharuraṭṭha*), who caused a rift between holy men (*isīnam antaram katvā*) and was consequently utterly ruined and destroyed along with his entire kingdom [Fausböll 1879; Sarkisyanz 1965]. The second verse draws the moral conclusion that the wise do not praise acting under the sway of partiality (*chandāgamanam na-ppasaṁsanti paṇḍitā*), admonishing that one should speak truthful, well-intentioned words without malice [Fausböll 1879]. In the story's conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies himself as having been the senior hermit (*jeṭṭhakaisi*) of that time [Fausböll 1879]. Later commentarial traditions in the *Jātaka* literature cite the *Bharujātaka* alongside stories such as the *Khantivādi-*, *Mātaṅga-*, and *Cetiyajātaka* as classic examples of the catastrophic ruin brought upon rulers through heedlessness and ethical misconduct [Fausböll 1891].

 DharmaNexus records Pali-internal text reuse with the commentary tradition, matching segments §0.4–2.4 of the verse text with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo) (§1092–1096), reflecting the preservation of the verses within their standard exegetical apparatus [DharmaNexus].
